design_detail: Two-week inpatient, double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-participant laboratory study with dose order counterbalanced across participants: 11 adults who used methamphetamine regularly by the intranasal route and were not seeking treatment each completed four two-day blocks (placebo and three active doses). Sleep was measured on the night after the dose (wrist actigraphy in 6 of 11; morning questionnaire in all 11), and next-morning plasma methamphetamine, heart rate, blood pressure, mood ratings and a psychomotor and memory battery were taken to assess 'residual' effects. Same participants as the acute-effects report Hart et al. (hart_2008).
can_establish: Within these 11 people, whether a single laboratory dose, compared with placebo, changes measured and self-rated sleep that night and mood, heart rate, blood pressure and test performance the next morning, and whether those changes depend on dose.
cannot_establish: What happens after repeated doses or binges over several days (the usual pattern the authors describe), after other routes, with street product, alongside alcohol or other drugs, or in people who are not experienced; objective sleep in the five participants whose actigraphy was lost; and whether small next-day effects on performance were missed (11 people, one morning test, no performance data shown).

sample.recruitment: Not described in this report beyond non-treatment-seeking adults studied as inpatients at the New York State Psychiatric Institute; the same participants are described in the acute-effects report (Hart et al.).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: DSM-IV current methamphetamine abuse or dependence, not seeking treatment; no other Axis I disorder; passed medical and psychiatric evaluation; normal weight range (2.1 Participants).
sample.demographics: Age 22 to 45 (mean 30.7); body mass index 24.1 (SD 4.4); methamphetamine used 3.6 (SD 1.7) days a week, mainly intranasally (nine had also smoked it, one injected). Six also used cocaine, seven alcohol, seven cannabis, and eight smoked tobacco (2.1 Participants).
sample.attrition: All 11 completed. Actigraphy data for the first five participants were lost through equipment malfunction (2.3 Sleep Monitoring).
sample.selection_effects: Experienced, non-treatment-seeking people who use mainly intranasally and agreed to a two-week inpatient study; screened free of other psychiatric disorders. Missing actigraphy was due to equipment, so it is unlikely to be related to the outcome, but it leaves objective sleep in only six people.

exposure.measurement: Doses given by the investigators under double-blind conditions in an inpatient unit; plasma methamphetamine measured the next morning.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: single intranasal doses of 0 (lactose placebo), 12, 25 and 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine hydrochloride (NIDA), each made up to 60 mg/70 kg with lactose and insufflated through a straw within 30 seconds; maximum single dose capped at 60 mg, so three participants over 84 kg received 41 to 48 mg/70 kg. Dose at about 10:00 on day 1 of each block; lights out at 23:00 for an 8-hour sleep period (about 13 hours after dosing); next-morning measures from about 10:00 on day 2 (about 24 hours after dosing). Blocks separated by at least 48 hours (Methods) or at least 24 hours (abstract). Next-morning plasma methamphetamine: 6.72, 13.67 and 38.08 ng/ml after the three active doses.
exposure.polysubstance: Inpatient residence from at least two days before the first session was intended to ensure washout and prevent other drug use during the study; current cocaine, alcohol, cannabis and tobacco use reported at entry (tobacco use during the study not described).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Admitted at least two days before the first session and resident throughout; no drug testing during the stay is described.

comparison.matching: Within-person; dose order counterbalanced (method not described).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the within-person comparison; habitual sleep and its baseline were not measured or reported.

outcomes.instruments: Actiwatch wrist actigraphy (total sleep time, awakenings; 6 participants); morning estimate of hours slept and six 100-mm visual analogue sleep items (slept well, woke early, fell asleep easily, clear-headed, woke often, satisfied); computerized visual analogue mood, drug-effect, physical-symptom and craving items; Digit-Symbol Substitution, repeated acquisition, divided attention, rapid information processing and digit recall tasks; heart rate, systolic and diastolic pressure; plasma methamphetamine.
outcomes.validity_norms: Actigraphy is a validated proxy for sleep but not polysomnography; the visual analogue items are laboratory-specific; no norms.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Residual' effects were defined by the authors as effects present once plasma levels are falling and acute effects are negligible (their time threshold is given in the exposure field); sleep disruption as shorter total sleep, more awakenings and worse ratings.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The number of subjective items and task measures analysed is not stated (the questionnaire is described only by example); Table 1 shows 6 sleep items, 6 of the mood ratings and 4 physiological measures.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind dosing; outcomes were self-ratings, task scores and devices. Blinding integrity was not assessed, and the higher doses have noticeable acute effects.

analysis.effect_sizes: Repeated-measures ANOVA with planned comparisons against placebo (Huynh-Feldt), df 1 and 30 for the 11-person measures. Actigraphy (n = 6): total sleep 4.4 against 6.4 hours with the highest dose (p < .01; '±' values 1.03 and 1.16 unlabelled); more awakenings with the highest dose than with any other condition (p < .01). Self-estimated sleep: 7.70 (SEM 0.31) hours after placebo, 6.77 (0.56), 4.83 (0.85) and 2.84 (0.89) after the three active doses, so about 2.9 and 4.9 hours less after the two higher doses (p < .001). 'Woke often' 16.50 (6.66) against 64.80 (12.48) and 67.56 (11.52); 'slept well' 85.20 (3.82) against 49.60 (11.68) and 21.44 (7.41). Next morning after the highest dose: alert 38.09 against 55.55, content 37.36 against 53.91, friendly 43.00 against 65.00, social 40.82 against 67.09, talkative 37.36 against 58.46 (all marked p < .05 against placebo); heart rate 90.46 against 78.36 bpm, systolic 124.00 against 118.00 and diastolic 78.55 against 69.00 mm Hg. Standardized effects and confidence intervals are not reported.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only selected subjective items are tabulated; 'depressed', 'anxious' and 'I want meth' are reported in the discussion as unchanged without values; no numbers at all are given for the five performance tasks.
analysis.power: Not addressed; 11 participants, 6 for objective sleep.

interpretation_gap.results_show: After the highest dose, measured sleep that night was about 2 hours shorter with more awakenings (6 people); after the two higher doses, people reported far less and worse sleep (11 people). The next morning, after the highest dose, several positive mood ratings were lower, heart rate and blood pressure were higher and methamphetamine was still in the blood; ratings of feeling depressed or anxious or wanting methamphetamine did not change, and no effect on the performance tasks was detected.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and discussion are mostly faithful. Gaps: (1) the discussion's statement that self-reports "may dramatically overestimate" sleep disruption compares 11 people's reports with 6 people's actigraphy, and actigraphy itself is only a proxy for sleep; (2) the absence of next-day performance effects is stated without data, from one morning test in 11 people, which can show only that no large effect was found; (3) next-day mood changes are summarized as limited although five of six tabulated positive-mood ratings fell after the highest dose. The authors themselves name the single-dose design, the six actigraphy records and the single morning test as limits.

timeline.event: Hart et al., acute physiological and behavioural effects of the same doses in the same participants.
This report of next-night and next-day effects: the first controlled study of residual effects of intranasal methamphetamine, by the authors' account.

replication.where_it_stands: A single small study; no replication with polysomnography, repeated dosing or a full next-day test schedule was found in the material read. The same participants appear in hart_2008, so the two reports are one sample.

funding.funder: Not reported in the PMC author manuscript (no acknowledgements or funding section). Methamphetamine was provided by the National Institute on Drug Abuse; the paper is an NIH author manuscript (NIHMS41862).
funding.affiliations_note: Columbia University and New York State Psychiatric Institute (Hart, Foltin, Gunderson and colleagues).

what_would_settle_it: A larger crossover study with polysomnography in every participant, single and repeated doses over consecutive days at the times people actually use, and next-day mood, performance and driving tests repeated through the day, with all outcomes pre-registered and reported.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the four dose conditions)
domains.note: Dose order counterbalanced; the scheme is not described.

Single doses with a washout between blocks (the abstract and Methods give different minimum gaps; exposure field); carry-over unlikely to be large, though next-morning plasma levels show the drug was still present the following day.
Double-blind with a lactose placebo, but the higher doses produce noticeable effects and blinding integrity was not checked; this matters for the self-rated sleep and mood outcomes.
Actigraphy missing for 5 of 11 through equipment failure (unlikely to depend on the outcome), leaving objective sleep in 6; other outcomes complete.
Objective actigraphy and vital signs are at low risk; the sleep and mood ratings are self-reports by participants who may have recognised the dose.
No protocol; only selected subjective items are tabulated and the performance results are reported without numbers.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Several domains raise some concerns, none high; the objective outcomes (actigraphy, heart rate, blood pressure, plasma level) carry less risk than the self-rated sleep and mood outcomes. Judged some concerns overall rather than high because the main effects are large and dose-related and the objective and subjective sleep measures point the same way. May be cited for the size and direction of next-night sleep loss and next-morning mood and cardiovascular changes after a single laboratory dose in experienced people; not for the absence of next-day cognitive effects, which rests on unreported data.

key_findings.finding: Measured sleep (actigraphy, 6 participants): after the highest dose, total sleep that night was 4.4 hours against 6.4 hours after placebo, an average reduction of 2 hours (p < .01), and awakenings were more frequent than after any other condition (p < .01); the two lower doses did not significantly change measured sleep.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1 Sleep, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 legend (left panels, n = 6)

key_findings.finding: Self-rated sleep (11 participants): estimated hours slept 7.70 (SEM 0.31) after placebo, 6.77 (0.56), 4.83 (0.85) and 2.84 (0.89) after the three active doses, about 2.9 and 4.9 hours less after the two higher doses (p < .001); after both higher doses people also rated falling asleep less easily, sleeping less well, waking more often and being less satisfied with their sleep, and after the highest dose feeling less clear-headed.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1 Sleep, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, sleep questionnaire rows

key_findings.finding: Next morning after the highest dose, ratings were lower than after placebo for alert (38.09 against 55.55), content (37.36 against 53.91), friendly (43.00 against 65.00), social (40.82 against 67.09) and talkative (37.36 against 58.46); energetic (22.80 against 35.20) is marked as different only from the lowest active dose. 'Social' was also lower after the lowest dose (50.36; F = 4.46, marked p < .05).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2 Subjective effects; Table 1, subjective-effect rows

key_findings.finding: Ratings of feeling depressed, feeling anxious and wanting methamphetamine were not changed by the previous day's dose (no values reported).

No significant next-day effect on the cognitive and psychomotor battery (digit-symbol substitution, repeated acquisition, divided attention, rapid information processing, immediate and delayed digit recall); no means or test statistics are reported.

The next morning, after the highest dose, heart rate was 90.46 against 78.36 bpm after placebo, systolic pressure 124.00 against 118.00 and diastolic 78.55 against 69.00 mm Hg (all p < .05), and plasma methamphetamine was still measurable after every active dose.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.4 Physiological measures; Table 1, physiological rows

key_findings.finding: Measured and self-rated awakenings after the highest dose were correlated at r = -.89 (p < .02, n = 6); there were no significant correlations after the middle dose. The authors read the gap between about 5 fewer self-reported and 2 fewer measured hours as self-report overestimating sleep loss.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and the Methods give different minimum gaps between the dose blocks (the abstract's is half the Methods'; values in the exposure field).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; 2.2 Design and Procedures, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The washout cannot be stated with certainty; with the shorter gap, methamphetamine from the previous block could still be measurable at the next dose, since it was measurable the morning after every active dose.

reporting_issues.issue: The correlation between measured awakenings and 'woke often' ratings after the highest dose is printed as r = -.89: a negative sign means that people with more measured awakenings reported waking less often. The text calls the measures significantly correlated without discussing the direction (n = 6, df 4).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the sign is a typographical error or the two measures disagreed person by person; the correlation cannot be used as agreement between self-report and actigraphy.

reporting_issues.issue: Significance marks in Table 1 do not follow the F values consistently: with df 1 and 30, F = 4.33 (unmarked, twice) and F = 4.38 (marked) both correspond to p of about .045 (editors' calculation); 'energetic' after the highest dose has F = 5.33 (p about .03) but is marked only as different from the lowest dose, while the text lists it among ratings significantly decreased.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1; Results › 3.2 Subjective effects
reporting_issues.consequence: Borderline effects (next-morning heart rate after the middle dose, 'energetic') cannot be classified with confidence; the main effects are far from the threshold and unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion contrasts nearly 5 fewer self-reported hours with 2 fewer measured hours, but the self-reports come from all 11 participants and the measured hours from 6; the same-person comparison is shown only in an image (Figure 1, right panels).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Figure 1 legend
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of any self-report overestimate is not established; part of the gap may reflect who had actigraphy.

reporting_issues.issue: The measured total sleep values (4.4 '±' 1.03 against 6.4 '±' 1.16 hours) do not say whether the spread is an SD or an SEM; elsewhere the paper uses SEM.
reporting_issues.consequence: A standardized effect cannot be computed reliably.

reporting_issues.issue: No funding or conflict-of-interest statement appears in the PMC author manuscript.
reporting_issues.consequence: Funding cannot be stated from the source read; the published version may carry it.
